title: Alapin Sicilian | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We know we're facing the Sicilian — c5.
We play c3 — the Alapin, which I recommend to every beginner; it's positionally very healthy.
Black plays e6, contesting the center.
We play d4.
Black plays d5 — now a choice: e5 into an Advance French, or capture.
We go the traditional Alapin way and capture on d5, letting Black choose how to recapture.
Black recaptures with the pawn — this heads toward an isolated-queen's-pawn structure, since we'll eventually take on c5 and leave Black an isolated d5 pawn. No rush to take c5 yet — develop first.
A knight to f3. The rule of thumb is to wait for Black to develop the dark-squared bishop and only then capture on c5, to make him lose a tempo.
Then a bishop check on b5 and castle, taking on c5 only when the f8 bishop moves.
A bishop check on b5, developing with tempo. Trades favor the side playing against the IQP — the more pieces come off, the weaker the pawn.
Black blocks with a bishop to d7.
A retreat with b6 isn't scary — Black avoids the IQP but at the cost of development.
We trade on d7, then castle.
Black recaptures and we castle — the main line; White is slightly better, a chance to show fundamentals.
Black plays a bishop to e7. He's positioned the knight so that after a capture on c5 he can retake with the knight — but we still want the IQP, even without winning the tempo.
We capture on c5.
A bishop to c5 would allow a rook check on e1, which Black doesn't want.
Assuming the recapture on c5 — the bishop to c5 allows the rook to e1 with check, which Black certainly won't want to allow.
Black takes with the bishop on c5 — a bad move. The three good bishop squares were e3, f4, and g5. Now there's a rook check on e1, and I suspect he's planning a knight to e4 in reply.
A rook check on e1. If a knight to e4, Black loses contact with the d5 pawn and we play a queen capture on d5 — after a bishop capture on f2 with check, keep calculating.
So a knight to e4, a queen capture on d5, a bishop capture on f2 with check — but we move the king to f1, Black takes the rook, and we assess.
It's going to be two pieces for a rook.
The king steps to f1 — very good for us.
Black takes on e1 and we play a queen capture on e4 with check — then trade queens and pick up the bishop, two pieces for a rook.
Black interposes a queen to e7.
We take the queen.
Black recaptures and we take the bishop with the king. Our knight is perfectly placed on f3, and we have two pieces for a rook — a material advantage we should convert.
Black plays a rook to e8. Two things to watch: a hole on d3 the knight wants, and the e-file under Black's control.

A bishop to e3, preventing a knight to c5 — and I'm not worried about the pin, because if the king moves we answer king to f2, getting out and defending the bishop. Concrete calculation supersedes a vague worry about a temporary pin.
The plan: king to f2, a knight to d2, then a knight to c4, and bring the rook in — once all our pieces are active, Black struggles to hold.
Black plays a knight to e5.
We trade. The key rule for two-pieces-versus-a-rook: the extra pair of rooks favors the side with the pieces.
We recapture on e5. The rooks let us keep the minors anchored, defending against side-to-side rook moves.
We develop the knight to d2.
Black plays a rook to e8. We can't move the bishop because of a rook to e2 — so a knight to c4 is the aim.
A rook to e1, bringing the rook in, ready to play a knight to f3 and chase the rook off e5.
Black plays f5, threatening f4.
But a knight to f3 comes with tempo, so we don't worry about f4.
A rook to b5. Instructive moment — a lot of people play b3 automatically, but see the bigger picture: b3 isn't the only way to defend the pawn.
I like b4, creating an anchor point for the bishop to reach c5.
Black plays b6 — the rook is almost trapped; if our pawn were on a3 we'd play c4. I have a clever move: a4 would trap the rook if not for a rook to d5.
So a rook to d1, guarding the d5 square and threatening a4 — I don't think Black has a defense.
Black plays f4 in desperation, giving up a pawn to open the rook's path.
We take on f4 — another pawn to the good, ready to infiltrate with a rook to d7.
Black plays a rook to f5.
A bishop to g3 — it truly doesn't matter which; this keeps the bishop solid and guards g5.
I don't like the bishop to d6, because it blocks the rook — don't play a move just because it comes with a check.
I like g3 — it solidifies the bishop and defends against g5; if h6, we play h4, the typical sequence.
Now down to business: we have a queenside pawn majority, so the fastest win is to create a passed pawn and promote it.
Not a4 — that lets Black ignore us. We play c4, and Black can't stop c5.
The easy way to know which pawn to push is where your extra pawn actually is.
It's the c-pawn that's extra, so that's the one to push.
We want to push the pawn — and find the move with a bit of tactics, not assuming anything automatically.
Using a little tactics — c5 is possible, because after Black takes we have a bishop to d6 with a fork, classic stuff with such an active bishop.
Black plays a king to g8. My minor pieces supervise the pawn, so I needn't put the rook behind it.
A rook to d5 — normally you'd put the rook behind the pawn, but here I value d-file control more, and there's no rush to push.
The b-pawns come off and we recapture with the pawn — I like a knight to d4 followed by c6.
Black plays a rook to b7, defending well, but we grind him down. In these endgames you must be ready to give away a couple of pawns to promote your passer.
c6 — after a rook takes on c6, we have a rook to d8 with check driving the king out, then a knight to e5 picks up the rook, so it's safe. Black can grab a2, but our pawn is essentially home free.
As you push the passer and give away your other pawns, beware the swindle: the opponent grabbing them all, then giving the rook for the passer at the end.
A king to e3 — I don't go to g1 in these situations, since it risks a ladder mate. c7 is coming.
Why king to e3 and not g1? Because g1 locks the king on the first rank with ladder-mate potential.
The rook to c2 locks our king on the first rank and threatens a ladder mate — which I don't want; so we push the pawn to c7.
c7 — and the game is over.
A rook to d8 — perhaps not the most accurate.
We could have finessed with a rook check on d7 and rerouted the knight.
But we know we win a full piece, so let's just go for it — Black resigns.

Everything was natural until the capture on c5. The bishop capture on c5 was just bad. On the IQP: the crucial thing is to control the square in front of the pawn as much as possible — a knight to d4 comes to mind, but you don't have to rush it; you already control d5, and can add a bishop to e3 and a knight to d2 first, planting a piece on d4 when the time is right. White is slightly better.
